bai.ten: Free fall is the straightest path
bai.moTa: A ball thrown upward travels “straight” across a curved spacetime
bai.yChinh: Embed the “time × height” part of the spacetime around Earth as a curved surface, and the world line of a ball thrown up and falling back turns out to be the **straightest line** (a geodesic) on that surface. No gravitational force pulls the ball; it is the person standing on the ground who is pushed off the straightest line. Most of the effect comes from **time** running at different rates at different heights.
bai.conSo.1: **1.09 × 10⁻¹⁶ per meter**: how much clock rates change with height at the ground (g/c²).
bai.conSo.2: **2.02 seconds, 5.0 m**: a ball thrown up at 9.9 m/s and falling back; general relativity and Newton agree to a few parts per million.
bai.conSo.3: **11.19 km/s**: escape velocity at Earth’s surface.
bai.conSo.4: **6,340 km**: the height reached when thrown straight up at 7.9 km/s.
bai.hieuDung: **Gravity does not pull the ball down.** The ball follows the straightest path through curved spacetime; it is the person standing on the ground who gets pushed (the ground pushes up at 9.8 m/s²). The curved surface in this lesson preserves only the geodesics, not the spacetime intervals, and it is hugely exaggerated.
bai.nguon: Surface construction: R. Jonsson, “Embedding spacetime via a geodesically equivalent metric of Euclidean signature,” Gen. Rel. Grav. 33, 1207 (2001). World lines computed from the Schwarzschild metric (Hartle 2003, ch. 9). Constants: CODATA 2018, Earth’s GM 3.986004418 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², standard g 9.80665 m/s². Optical clocks: Chou et al. 2010, Science 329, 1630; Bothwell et al. 2022, Nature 602, 420.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Read the spacetime surface (time × height): going around the axis is time, going along the surface is height.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Explain why the world line of a ball thrown upward is a geodesic, while that of a person standing still is not.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Say why every object, heavy or light, falls along the same path.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Derive g = (c²/2)·dA/dr from how clock rates change with height, and compute g/c² ≈ 1.09 × 10⁻¹⁶ per meter.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Know what the model gets exactly right and what it does not.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: No gravity: time wrapped around a cylinder
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
You are looking at a **cylinder**. It is a piece of {{không-thời gian|spacetime}} with only two dimensions: **height** (along the cylinder, from bottom to top) and **time** (around the cylinder). Every point on it is an {{sự kiện|event}}: “at this height, at this moment.” In Lesson 4 we stood the time axis upright; here we **wrap** it around the cylinder, so that in a moment the cylinder can change shape.

The green line is the **“now”** meridian; it turns steadily around the cylinder. The column on the left is the familiar view: height only, no time. The ball on the column sits at exactly the height where its world line crosses the “now” meridian.

- A person standing still on the ground: the height never changes, but time still passes. The world line is **a circle** around the foot of the cylinder.
- A ball thrown up at 9.9 m/s where **there is no gravity**: every second it climbs another 9.9 m. Its world line is **a helix** that climbs forever and never comes back.

Cut the cylinder along a vertical line and unroll it: the helix becomes a **slanted straight line**, the circle a **horizontal straight line**. Both are straight lines: this is the uniform motion of Lesson 4.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the tip of the yellow arrow on the left column to throw harder or softer, or drag the white dot on the cylinder to change the starting direction of the world line: steeper means a faster throw.
> [[Throw at 9.9 m/s|nem]] [[Slow throw, 4 m/s|cham]] [[View from above|tren]] [[Oblique view|cheo]]

> [Lưu ý] Sound: while the ball flies you hear a tone whose pitch follows the rate of a clock at rest at the ball’s height. There is no gravity yet, so every clock ticks at the same rate and the tone keeps one pitch even as the ball climbs.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.de: Throw from the ground so that the helix reaches the rim of the cylinder (10 m) after **exactly one turn** around it (2.69 seconds). You succeed when the speed is within 0.12 m/s.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.goiY: On the cylinder the world line is straight, so the speed is constant: $v = 10\ \text{m} / 2{,}69\ \text{s} \approx 3{,}71$ m/s.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: Gravity on: the surface flares out at the bottom
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Now switch on Earth’s gravity. The cylinder **flares out at the bottom** and narrows toward the top. Why flare at the bottom? Lesson 9 tells us: a clock lower down runs **slower** than a clock higher up. The surface is built so that its straightest lines coincide with real falling paths, and for that to work the circles lower down must be wider than those higher up. Apart from two freely chosen drawing parameters (step 7), how much it flares depends on one thing: how quickly clock rates change with height. The stronger the gravity, the sharper the flare; with no gravity the surface goes back to being a cylinder. The surface color shows the clock rate: orange-yellow at the bottom (slow), blue at the top (fast).

> [Lưu ý] The arc length on the surface is **not** the number of seconds a clock at that height counts. The surface gets exactly one thing right, the path of a freely falling object; step 7 explains.

Throw the ball exactly as before, at 9.9 m/s. This time it no longer spirals upward forever. It climbs to 5 m and **comes back** to the ground after 2.02 seconds. The yellow ribbon is its true world line, computed from general relativity.

The remarkable part: we **added no force** to the model. We only changed the shape of the surface. The ball still goes “straight,” as it did on the cylinder; it is the curved surface that makes that straight line turn back.

> [Lưu ý] The flare is **enormously exaggerated**. Over 10 m of height, real clock rates differ by only about one part in a million billion ($1{,}09 \times 10^{-15}$). Section 7 explains how the model is exaggerated while still getting the ball’s path exactly right.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the tip of the yellow arrow on the left column to throw again: each throw is a new starting direction, and every path below escape velocity comes back to the ground.
> [[Gravity off|tat]] [[Gravity on|bat]] [[Throw at 9.9 m/s|nem]]

> [Lưu ý] Sound: the tone while the ball flies has a pitch that follows the rate of a clock at rest at the ball’s height. Going up, the tone rises; falling, it drops; landing makes a “thud.” The real rate difference over 10 m is only $1{,}09 \times 10^{-15}$; the sound is exaggerated so that the ground is 220 Hz and a height of 10 m is 440 Hz (an octave higher), with pitches in between proportional to the rate difference.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.ten: What the “straightest line” on a curved surface means
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
On a curved surface there are no straight lines in the ruler sense. But there is still a way to go “straight”: **never steer** left or right. An ant crawling on a ball that always puts each foot straight ahead traces out such a line. That line is called a {{đường trắc địa|geodesic}}.

A hands-on test: take **a straight strip of tape** and stick it on the surface. Tape refuses to bend sideways, so it lies along a geodesic by itself. The ball’s world line is drawn as a narrow ribbon with two parallel edges to suggest exactly that picture: stick a straight strip of tape from the foot of the surface, in the same starting direction, and it will lie right on this line.

> [Ví dụ] A flight from New York to Hong Kong swings up close to the North Pole, reaching latitude 84°. On a flat map the route looks curved, but on the globe it is a **great circle**, a geodesic of the sphere: the shortest path, and one that never steers.

On our surface, a geodesic heading toward the narrow end gradually leans over and then turns back toward the wide end, even though no one steers it: that follows from the surface narrowing (Clairaut’s relation, in the “Go deeper” section below). Whether two balls thrown side by side gradually converge or spread apart is what reveals true curvature; Lesson 12 covers that.

> [Thử ngay] Hover over the small ball running along the surface to read its flight time; rotate the surface to see the ribbon from several sides.
> [[Close-up of the ribbon|gan]] [[Full view|cheo]]

+++ Go deeper: checking a geodesic with Clairaut’s relation
On a surface of revolution there is a very neat test for geodesics. Let $\rho$ be the radius of the circle at a point on the path, and $\gamma$ the angle between the path and the meridian there. Clairaut’s relation says that along a geodesic,

$$ C = \rho \sin\gamma $$

is **constant**. Moving up toward the narrow part, $\rho$ shrinks, so $\sin\gamma$ must grow: the path leans over toward horizontal (the speed drops). Where $\sin\gamma = 1$ the path runs parallel to the circle: that is the top, where the ball stops. After that the path turns down.

The lesson’s numerical checks compute $C$ along the ball’s true world line (solved from general relativity, using nothing from the surface). $C$ stays constant to about $10^{-14}$, both for Earth and right next to a black hole. So the ribbon in the picture really is a geodesic of the surface.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: Standing still is NOT the straightest path
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The orange-red circle at the foot of the surface is the world line of **a person standing still on the ground**. On the cylinder that circle was a straight line. On the flared surface it is not: a circle where the surface is flaring out always has to **steer** to one side. To travel along it, something has to keep pushing.

That push comes from **the ground** (the floor, the soles of your shoes). The orange-red arrows show the direction of the push: upward, with an acceleration of 9.8 m/s². We call the feeling of being pushed **weight**.

If the ground vanished and nothing pushed any more, we would follow the straightest path: we would fall. Try it with a ball held at a height of 5 m (the upper orange-red circle). Let go, and the world line leaves the circle in exactly the circle’s direction, then goes “straight” down to the ground.

> [Tóm lại] Free fall is the state of **feeling no force at all**, just like an astronaut floating weightless (Lesson 7). Standing still on the ground is the state of **being pushed**, like standing in a rocket that is accelerating (Lesson 8).

> [Thử ngay] Drag the faint ball on the left column up or down to change the release height.
> [[Drop from 5 m|tha5]] [[Drop from 9 m|tha9]] [[Gravity off: the circle is straight again|tat]] [[Gravity back on|bat]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the faint ball on the left column to a height from which, once released, it hits the ground after **exactly 1.2 seconds** (within 0.03 seconds).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: Newton gives $h = \tfrac12 g t^2 = \tfrac12 \times 9{,}8 \times 1{,}2^2 \approx 7{,}1$ m. Read the flight time in the readout at the bottom corner.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: Hard throws, soft throws, heavy or light
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Each way of throwing is a different starting direction from the same event at the foot of the surface. The harder the throw, the steeper the ribbon starts out, the higher it climbs, and the longer it takes to come back.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the tip of the yellow arrow to throw one yourself.
> [[Throw at 4, 7, 10 and 13 m/s|bon]] [[Heavy ball and light ball|nang]] [[Drop from 8 m|tha]]

Press “Heavy ball and light ball”: a shot put and a ping-pong ball are thrown at the same speed. The two ribbons **coincide exactly**. The path is set by the geometry of the surface, and geometry does not know whether an object is heavy or light. This is just what Galileo saw: all objects (ignoring air resistance) fall the same way. For Newton this was a strange coincidence (inertial mass equals gravitational mass); for Einstein it is obvious.

Switch to the **Around Earth** scale (from the ground up to 4 Earth radii) to throw really hard:

- 7.9 km/s straight up: the ball reaches a height of about 6,340 km and falls back after 69 minutes.
- 11.2 km/s is the {{tốc độ thoát|escape velocity}}: the ribbon climbs forever and never returns.

> [Thử ngay] [[Throw at 7.9 km/s|v79]] [[Throw at 11.2 km/s|v112]] [[Back to the backyard|san]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: At the “Backyard” scale, throw straight up from the ground so that the ball flies for **exactly 2 seconds** before landing (within 0.03 seconds).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: Going up takes half the time, and every second the ball loses 9.8 m/s of speed: $v \approx 9{,}8$ m/s.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: Why curved time is all you need
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
The rings of text on the surface now show the **clock rate** at each height, compared with the ground. At 10 m a clock runs faster than one on the ground by only a tiny fraction: $1{,}09 \times 10^{-15}$, about one part in a million billion. How can such a small number bend the ball’s path?

The answer lies in the units. In spacetime, every second we travel **300,000 km** along the time axis ($c \times 1$ second), while the ball moves only a few meters through space. Its world line lies almost entirely along the time axis, so a very small difference in the rate of time, multiplied by that enormous distance, is enough to bend it visibly.

The neat result: the acceleration of falling equals $c^2/2$ times how much $A = 1 - r_s/r$ changes per meter:

$$ g = \frac{c^2}{2}\,\frac{\dd A}{\dd r} $$

$$ g = c^2 \times \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\big(\text{clock rate}\big) $$

Plugging in: the clock rate changes by $1{,}09 \times 10^{-16}$ per meter; multiply by $c^2 = 8{,}99 \times 10^{16}$ m²/s² and you get $g = 9{,}8$ m/s².

> [Con số] Today’s optical atomic clocks can measure this difference when a clock is raised by just a few tens of centimeters (Chou et al. 2010), or even by one millimeter (Bothwell et al. 2022).

> [Thử ngay] Throw and listen: the tone rises and then falls with the clock rate at the ball’s height, just like the rings of text on the surface (the difference is exaggerated, see step 2).
> [[Throw at 9.9 m/s|nem]] [[Drop from 10 m|tha]]

+++ Go deeper: deriving g from the equation of motion, line by line
With $c = 1$, the true world line of an object thrown vertically satisfies (see the Formulas section):

$$ \frac{\dd^2 r}{\dd t^2} = \frac{A\,A'\,(2W - A)}{2E^2} $$

$$ A' = \frac{\dd A}{\dd r} = \frac{r_s}{r^2} $$

where $W = E^2 - A$ and $(\dd r/\dd t)^2 = A^2 W/E^2$.

1. **Low speed**: $(\dd r/\dd t)^2 = A^2W/E^2 \ll 1$, so $W \ll A$; drop $2W$ next to $A$: $\ \ddot r \approx -A^2 A'/(2E^2)$.
2. Also because $W \ll A$, $E^2 = A + W \approx A$: $\ \ddot r \approx -A\,A'/2$.
3. **Weak field**: $A = 1 - r_s/r \approx 1$ (for Earth $r_s/R = 1{,}4 \times 10^{-9}$): $\ \ddot r \approx -A'/2 = -r_s/(2r^2)$.
4. Substitute $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ and restore $c$: $\ \ddot r = -\dfrac{c^2}{2}\,\dfrac{\dd A}{\dd r} = -\dfrac{GM}{r^2}$. This is exactly Newton’s law.

The clock rate of someone standing still is $\sqrt{A} \approx 1 - r_s/(2r)$, so the change in rate per meter is $\tfrac12 \dd A/\dd r = g/c^2 = 9{,}807/(2{,}998 \times 10^8)^2 = 1{,}09 \times 10^{-16}$ per meter.

The spatial part of the metric ($B = 1/A$) only enters the term containing $(\dd r/\dd t)^2$, which is smaller by a factor of about $v^2/c^2 \approx 10^{-15}$. So for any slow motion, **the curvature of time** produces almost all of gravity.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
This model gets **one thing** exactly right: the geodesics of the surface coincide with the world lines of objects falling freely along the vertical (and of light moving vertically). Everything else is a way of drawing.

- The surface **does not preserve spacetime intervals**: length on the surface is not proper time. The surface is built from a “dual” metric that differs from the real metric but has the same geodesics (Jonsson’s method, 2001).
- The shape of the surface has **two freely chosen parameters** (flare and height). Change them and the surface gets fatter or thinner, but the ball still follows the correct geodesic.
- Time **wraps around**: after one turn the surface lands on itself. Only read paths shorter than one turn.
- For the real Earth the curvature is extremely small; the picture is exaggerated so you can see it.

Near a black hole the true curvature is already large: from $r = 1{,}5\,r_s$ to $8\,r_s$ the clock rate goes from 0.58 to 0.94 times the rate far away, and the colors on the surface are real, not exaggerated.

> [Thử ngay] At the “Near a black hole” scale, drag the yellow arrow to throw from $1{,}5\,r_s$ and see where the ribbon turns back.
> [[Near a black hole|ld]] [[Around Earth|td]] [[Backyard|san]]

This surface has only time and one height dimension. **Lesson 11** covers the spatial part of curvature (rulers measuring longer around a mass). **Lesson 12** covers true curvature, the kind no change of frame can remove: tidal forces.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.de: At the “Near a black hole” scale, throw straight up from $1{,}5\,r_s$ so that the ball rises to **exactly $3\,r_s$** and falls back (within $0{,}2\,r_s$).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.goiY: Energy is conserved: $A(r_{\text{peak}}) = A(r_0)/(1 - \beta^2)$ with $A = 1 - r_s/r$. Put in $r_0 = 1{,}5\,r_s$, $r_{\text{peak}} = 3\,r_s$: $1 - \beta^2 = \tfrac12$, $\beta \approx 0{,}71\,c$ (measured locally).
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: $t$ is the time of a clock very far away, $r$ is the radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ (Earth: 8.9 mm). A clock at rest at $r$ ticks at rate $\sqrt A$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.ten: World line of an object thrown vertically
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: $\psi = A(r) - A(R)$, $B = 1/A$, $\delta > 0$, $k = A(R) - \delta$. This positive-definite metric has the same geodesics as the real metric; the surface of revolution has radius $a = \sqrt{A/(A(R)(1 + \psi/\delta))}$ and angle $\varphi = t/T_0$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: Along a geodesic on a surface of revolution: $\rho$ is the radius of the circle, $\gamma$ the angle between the path and the meridian.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: On this lesson’s spacetime surface, the world line of a person standing on the ground is the circle at the foot of the surface. Why is it NOT a geodesic when there is gravity?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.1: Because a person standing still has no world line
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: Because where the surface flares, the circle has to keep steering; only with the ground pushing can you travel along it
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.4: Because the person standing still moves faster than the ball
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: A circle where the radius of the surface is changing always curves to one side relative to the surface (Clairaut’s relation: only a circle where the radius reaches an extremum is a geodesic). On the cylinder (no gravity) the circle is a geodesic again. The circle is closed only because time was wrapped around when drawing.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: A shot put and a ping-pong ball are thrown up at the same speed, ignoring air. What does the model show?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.1: The shot put rises less because it is heavier
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.2: The ping-pong ball falls more slowly
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.3: The two world lines coincide, because a geodesic depends only on the starting point and direction
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.4: The two paths cross at the top
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: A geodesic is completely determined by its starting event and starting direction (that is, its velocity). Mass appears nowhere in the geometry. This is how general relativity explains Galileo’s observation.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: A clock at height $h$ runs faster than a clock on the ground by a fraction $gh/c^2$. What is that fraction for $h = 100$ m?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: $g/c^2 = 9{,}81/(3 \times 10^8)^2 \approx 1{,}09 \times 10^{-16}$ per meter; times 100 m gives $1{,}09 \times 10^{-14}$. The first option is the figure for one meter.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: An astronaut floats weightless in a space station, and a person stands on the ground. Who is following a geodesic of spacetime?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: The person on the ground, because they are standing still
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: The astronaut, because no force acts on them except “gravity,” and gravity is not a force
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: The astronaut is in free fall (around Earth), so follows a geodesic and feels no weight. The person on the ground is pushed off the geodesic by the ground with an upward acceleration of 9.8 m/s²; that feeling of being pushed is weight.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Can this curved-surface model give you the ball’s proper time if you measure the length of the ribbon?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.1: Yes, the length of the ribbon is the proper time
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: No: the surface preserves only geodesics, not spacetime intervals
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.3: Yes, but you have to multiply by c
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: The surface is built from a positive-definite metric that differs from the real one and only shares its geodesics. Length on the surface is not proper time. To compute proper time you have to use the real metric.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Why is a difference in clock rates as tiny as 10⁻¹⁶ per meter enough to produce an acceleration of 9.8 m/s²?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: Because the ball travels through spacetime mostly along the time direction: each second is 300,000 km along the time axis, compared with a few meters in space. The acceleration equals $c^2$ times the change in clock rate per meter: $g = c^2 \times 1{,}09 \times 10^{-16}\ \text{m}^{-1} = 8{,}99 \times 10^{16} \times 1{,}09 \times 10^{-16} \approx 9{,}8$ m/s². The huge factor $c^2$ makes up for the tiny curvature.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: R. Jonsson, “Embedding spacetime via a geodesically equivalent metric of Euclidean signature,” Gen. Rel. Grav. 33, 1207 (2001): the surface construction used in this lesson.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 6 (gravity as geometry) and chapter 8 (geodesics).
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: E. F. Taylor, J. A. Wheeler and E. Bertschinger, *Exploring Black Holes* (2nd ed.): objects falling vertically around a black hole.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: K. S. Thorne, *Black Holes and Time Warps* (1994): why the curvature of time produces gravity.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: A surface drawn in ordinary three-dimensional space to represent part of a curved spacetime, keeping one chosen property exactly (in Lesson 10: the geodesics).
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: The smallest upward launch speed at which an object travels away forever without falling back. At Earth’s surface: 11.2 km/s.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: Along a geodesic on a surface of revolution, the radius of the circle times the sine of the angle between the path and the meridian stays constant.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: The acceleration an object itself feels and an accelerometer measures: 0 in free fall, 9.8 m/s² upward when standing on the ground.
